newsitem.title: USA: NBC says ratings stand not about money.
newsitem.headline: NBC says ratings stand not about money.

text.p: Warren Littlefield, the top programming executive at NBC, said that the network's refusal to join the new television ratings system was not prompted by a fear of losing ad dollars but by worries over censorship.
"Our motivation is not financial," Littlefield said at a presentation here on Saturday for critics and reporters. "It's a philosophical one."

Reporters peppered Littlefield, the president of NBC Entertainment, with questions over whether the network was afraid to join the new ratings system because it feared that top-rated shows such as "Friends" would get a ratings warning over adult dialogue and scare away potential advertisers.
Littlefield dismissed the assertion, emphatically saying that the network rejected the new system because it was a first step by politicians and special interest groups to control content.
Littlefield said the message from proponents of the system, which goes into effect later this year, is: "We don't want to control your garbage. We want to remove your garbage."
Littlefield said the ratings issue was the most frightening development he has seen in 20 years of broadcasting.
"It's a little snowball rolling downhill, and you're looking at a potential avalanche," he said.
The recently revised system will include letters flashed on TV screens to indicate programmes that contain sex, violence, adult dialogue and situations.
Littlefield spoke during the two-day presentation NBC uses to promote its new programmes for the fall season.

Asked whether NBC has been backing away from so-called quality programming, especially made-for-TV movies, he said, "I don't know if creative daring is the goal for us. I think our goal is entertaining as many people as we can."
He said the network was choosing "big event" movies and mini-series, such as "House of Frankenstein," which will air around Halloween.

Littlefield also said he was programming NBC, which is owned by General Electric Co., in a bid to distinguish the network from cable networks, which have stolen viewers from the broadcast networks for years.

"We don't want our movies to have the sameness" of other networks, he said. One way to distinguish NBC from cable networks was to develop original comedy and dramatic series, he said. NBC lost 10 percent of its audience in the 1996-97 season from a year ago, figures show.
Littlefield said the network's goal was to stop the erosion and begin to boost the audience. He used the word "growth" to describe the goal but declined to elaborate.
"Our goal is to bring as many eyeballs into the tent as we can," he said.
